title: The body scan
hook: moving attention from feet to head, central to Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR course (1979), drawn from Buddhist practice

segments.voice: Yesterday: Thoreau and the art of going nowhere in particular. Your line was saunter.

Quick question: how are your feet right now? You probably had to go and check. That's normal. Most of the day it's easy to live about six inches behind the eyes, with the rest of the body just carrying the head around. It only gets attention when it hurts. In 1979, in a hospital in Worcester, Massachusetts, a scientist named Jon Kabat-Zinn started a course for patients with chronic pain and illness that doctors had run out of ways to help. One of the first things he taught them was to lie down and visit their own bodies, one part at a time, starting at the toes.
screen: `HOW ARE YOUR FEET?` → `A HOSPITAL, 1979.` → `THE BODY SCAN.`

segments.voice: The course was called Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, MBSR for short, begun at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center. It's eight weeks long, and the body scan sits right at the start. You lie on your back and move your attention slowly: the toes of the left foot, the sole, the heel, the ankle, up the leg, then the right, the hips, the belly, the back, the hands, the arms, the shoulders, the neck, the face, the top of the head. At each place you simply notice. Warm, cold, tingling, aching, nothing at all. Nothing at all counts too. You're not trying to relax, though that often happens. You're trying to be there. Kabat-Zinn was open about where he learned this: from Buddhist meditation, which he practiced for years before shaping it for a hospital. The roots go deep. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha's great teaching on mindfulness, one exercise is to review this very body from the soles of the feet up, and from the crown of the head down. The word in Pali is kayagatasati, mindfulness of the body. MBSR set the religious framing aside so anyone could use it, and it's been studied a great deal since, with real but moderate benefits for stress. You spend all day living in your body. The scan is a way of showing up there on purpose, and saying, part by part: here I am.
screen: `MBSR: EIGHT WEEKS, 1979.` · `TOES TO THE TOP OF THE HEAD.` · `NOT RELAXING: BEING THERE.` · `ROOTS IN BUDDHIST PRACTICE.` · then, large: `HERE I AM.`

segments.voice: Sitting or lying down, start at your feet and ask what's there, warmth, pressure or nothing, then move up through the legs, the belly rising and falling, the back, the hands, the shoulders, the jaw, the eyes and the top of the head. Don't fix anything; just visit. At the end, feel the whole body at once, and say inside: here I am.
Kayagatasati. The old Pali name for mindfulness of the body, attention moving slowly from the feet to the head, noticing without fixing. Today's word.
Your line: here I am. Your body is where you live all day. Day one hundred thirty-two, done.

howItsDone: In Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction courses, participants practice a guided body scan, usually lying down for about forty-five minutes, moving attention slowly through the body from the feet to the head.

original.note: Pali, kayagatasati: mindfulness (sati) gone to the body (kaya). the old name for attention to the body.

chat.says: What's the point of a body scan if you're not trying to relax?
options: To be there on purpose: notice each part, warm, achy or nothing, without fixing it.
To find the sore spots and fix them, the way a massage loosens a knot.
To fall asleep fast; the scan only works if you drift off by the end.
chat.meaning: In the body scan you simply notice, part by part. You're not trying to relax, though that often happens. You're trying to be there.

notes: Audit 2026-09-30: practice called a five-minute scan 'the long version' while howItsDone says the MBSR scan runs about forty-five minutes; now 'a slower one'. Replaced the stock phrase 'the quiet gift of it'.
Kabat-Zinn named and paraphrased, never quoted. Confirm MBSR began in 1979 at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center (Worcester).

MN 10's body-parts contemplation reviews the body 'up from the soles of the feet and down from the crown of the head'; paraphrased. The MBSR sweep is also often traced to the U Ba Khin / Goenka vipassana lineage; the script says only 'Buddhist meditation'.
'Real but moderate benefits for stress' summarizes meta-analyses of MBSR (e.g. Khoury et al. 2015); confirm the hedge is fair.
Carry keeps the index's capital 'I' (here I am).
